extracted.intended_audience: general readers of 19th-century literature and essays on antiquities
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of 19th-century short fiction and antiquarian literary essays (Irving-style sketches) that describe gothic tombs, commemorative monuments, and related aesthetic judgments. Useful for readers or critics assessing period prose, monument description, and attitudes toward memorial design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate tone for tomb monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: “The grave should be surrounded by everything that might inspire tenderness and veneration for the dead, or that might win the living to virtue. It is the place not of disgust and dismay, but of sorrow and meditation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monuments and funerary sculpture should aim to inspire tenderness, veneration, and reflection in the living rather than horror or disgust. Avoid grotesque or shocking imagery that distracts from mournful contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and proud expression in epitaphs
rubrics_metrics.description: “There was a noble way in former times of saying things simply, and yet saying them proudly; and I do not know an epitaph that breathes a loftier consciousness of family worth and honorable lineage than one which affirms of a noble house that ‘all the brothers were brave and all the sisters virtuous.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epitaphs are more effective when concise and dignified: favor simple, proud statements of virtue or lineage over long, ornate, or convoluted inscriptions. Clarity and measured pride are virtues in commemorative text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer solemn, reposeful effigies to overwrought allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is something extremely solemn and awful in those effigies on Gothic tombs, extended as if in the sleep of death or in the supplication of the dying hour. They have an effect infinitely more impressive on my feelings than the fanciful attitudes, the over wrought conceits, the allegorical groups which abound on modern monuments.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In sculptural treatment of the dead, a calm, reposeful attitude (sleeping or supplicatory) is recommended over dramatic, allegorical, or sensational compositions. Simplicity and solemnity produce greater emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity in literary memorials fosters intimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: “The monuments are generally simple, for the lives of literary men afford no striking themes for the sculptor. ... Notwithstanding the simplicity of these memorials, I have always observed that the visitors to the abbey remained longest about them. A kinder and fonder feeling takes place of that cold curiosity or vague admiration with which they gaze on the splendid monuments of the great and the heroic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorials to literary figures should favor modest, intimate forms (busts, inscriptions, medallions) rather than grandiose sculpture; such simplicity invites personal feeling and prolonged attention from visitors.
